title: Where the two walkers meet
allegory: Finding where a ray hits a segment is like sending two walkers, one along the torch beam and one along the plank, and solving for how far each must go to meet; if their paths are parallel they never meet, and that is an answer, not a crash.
map: the torch and the way it points
ray origin O and direction D
the plank from one post to the other
u, the ray parameter (a hit needs u ≥ 0)
v, the segment parameter (a hit needs 0 ≤ v ≤ 1)
walkers on parallel paths never meet
singular matrix, det ≈ 0: mark the ray as a miss

chapters.name: The dark field
chapters.note: a million beams, one question each

cap.1: You point a torch into the dark. Somewhere out there is a plank. Does the beam hit it, and where? Now ask that for a million beams at once.
cap.2: A ray is an origin O plus a direction D. A segment runs from L₁ to L₂. For every ray you want to know: does it cross the segment, and where? No Python loops allowed.
cap.3: Rays live in a (nrays, 2, 3) tensor: an origin and a direction, each a 3D point. The job is a vectorised hit test against segments, and then triangles.

cap.1: Send out two walkers. One strides along the beam, one walks along the plank. If they can meet, the beam hits. Each only needs one number: how far they went.
cap.2: Walker one stands at O + u·D after u steps along the ray. Walker two stands at L₁ + v·(L₂ − L₁), a fraction v of the way along the segment. A hit is a (u, v) where they coincide.
cap.3: Parametrise both: the ray as O + uD, the segment as L₁ + v(L₂ − L₁). Intersection means equal points: two scalar unknowns and, in 2D, two scalar equations.

cap.1: Write where each walker stands and demand the spots match. Across and up give two equations for two unknowns: a tiny puzzle a solver cracks instantly.
cap.2: Move the unknowns left: u·D + v·(L₁ − L₂) = L₁ − O. That is a 2x2 matrix with columns D and L₁ − L₂. torch.linalg.solve returns u and v; you never solve it by hand.
cap.3: [D | L₁−L₂]·[u, v]ᵀ = L₁ − O, using the x and y coordinates only. Batched, you stack one 2x2 matrix per (ray, segment) pair and call linalg.solve once over the stack.

cap.1: Two checks decide it. The beam walker must go forwards (u at least 0). The plank walker must stay on the plank (v from 0 to 1). Beam D never meets at all.
cap.2: Hit = (u >= 0) & (v >= 0) & (v <= 1). B crosses the line past L₂. C crosses behind the torch. D is parallel, so there is no solution to check.
cap.3: The solve finds where two infinite lines cross; the inequalities restrict it to the half-line u ≥ 0 and the segment v ∈ [0, 1]. For triangles the same idea becomes u, v ≥ 0 and u + v ≤ 1.

chapters.name: Parallel is an answer
chapters.verdict: Walkers on parallel paths never meet. That is a miss, not an error.

cap.1: If the beam runs parallel to the plank, the walkers never meet. The solver panics and throws. Nothing is broken: it is telling you 'miss'.
cap.2: Parallel means the 2x2 matrix is singular (determinant ≈ 0), and torch.linalg.solve raises. Detect near-zero determinants first and mark those rays as misses.
cap.3: Mask degenerate rows: where |det| < 1e-8, substitute the identity so the batched solve succeeds, then force those entries to False. It is the course's first degenerate batch element to handle rather than crash on.

cap.1: A classic slip: pull origins and directions apart along the wrong side. Nothing complains. The picture just comes out wrong, so trust shapes, not silence.
cap.2: rays.unbind(-1) splits the size-3 axis, not the size-2 one. Both are small, nothing raises, and the solve happily eats scrambled O and D. Use unbind(1) and read shapes in the debugger.
cap.3: Shape-valid, semantics-wrong: any traceback lands lines later, on linalg.solve. A jaxtyping signature like Float[Tensor, 'nrays rayPoints=2 dims=3'] makes the right axis readable before you run anything.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Batch a million small solves, no loops
A degenerate case is an answer, not a crash
Read shapes in the debugger, not prints

cap.1: The torch and plank are a warm-up. The habits stick: do it all at once, treat odd cases as answers, check shapes. You need all three to study AI models.
cap.2: Interpretability code runs the same op over thousands of prompts. One degenerate row must be masked, not allowed to crash the batch, and every axis must mean what you think.
cap.3: Masked batched ops over (batch, pos, d_model) caches, with named axes and debugger-checked shapes, are the daily mechanics of probing and patching models to understand and steer them.

coda.title: Aim the torch, tilt the plank

params.label: plank tilt (rise from L₁ to L₂)

curves.label: the plank's line (the plank runs x = 1 to 2)

readouts.label: verdict
readouts.f: abs(slope - tilt) < 1e-9 ? 'MISS: parallel, singular matrix' : ((0.2 - slope)/(slope - tilt) >= 0 && (0.2 - slope)/(slope - tilt) <= 1 && aim*(1 + (0.2 - slope)/(slope - tilt)) >= 0 ? 'HIT' : 'MISS')

caption.1: Tilt the plank until it matches the beam's slope: the answer becomes 'no solution'. Flip aim to -1: same line, but the plank is now behind you.
caption.2: Push slope up until v passes 1: the lines still cross, but past the plank's far end. Set slope equal to tilt and the determinant hits 0. With aim at -1, u goes negative: a crossing behind the torch.
caption.3: det = aim·(slope − tilt), zero exactly when D is parallel to L₂ − L₁. v = (0.2 − slope)/(slope − tilt) explodes near parallel; exactly parallel, linalg.solve raises, so mask small |det| first.

where_else: Ray-triangle hits: the same solve with three unknowns, read as barycentric coordinates
Collision detection in games and physics engines
Any batch of linear solves where a few matrices are singular: mask them, don't crash

hamming.what: Turning 'does this ray hit this segment?' into a 2x2 linear system whose two unknowns say how far along each line the crossing is.
hamming.when: Whenever you need geometric answers for many rays at once; in [0.1] it is the first real batched computation.
hamming.why: One batched solve replaces a loop of if-statements, and a parallel ray becomes a clean miss instead of a crash.

object.title: The pegboard of beams
object.subtitle: Every peg is one beam paired with one plank; tall pegs are hits.

knobs.label: height of the plank's near end

cap.1: Each peg is one beam paired with one plank. Rows are beam slopes, columns are plank tilts. A tall peg means that beam hits that plank.
cap.2: One peg per (ray, segment) pair: rows are ray slopes, columns are segment tilts. The whole board is one batched solve plus the u and v checks.
cap.3: An (nrays, nsegments) boolean table; each entry is one 2x2 solve followed by u ≥ 0 and 0 ≤ v ≤ 1.

cap.1: Look down the diagonal: a line of flat pegs. There the beam runs parallel to the plank, so the walkers never meet. A miss, not a crash.
cap.2: On the diagonal, beam slope equals plank tilt and the matrix is singular. It is masked as a miss instead of letting linalg.solve throw.
cap.3: det = slope − tilt vanishes on r = c. Masking |det| < ε before the solve keeps the batch alive and labels those pairs False.

cap.1: One whole row stands tall: that beam aims straight at the plank's near end, so it touches every plank except the parallel one.
cap.2: When the beam passes exactly through L₁, v = 0 for every tilt. The hit sits on the endpoint, and it counts because the check is v ≥ 0.
cap.3: For slope equal to L₁'s height, v = (a − s)/(s − t) = 0 for all t ≠ s. Endpoint inclusivity (≥, not >) decides whether these count.

cap.1: Raise the plank's near end. The tall row slides up to steeper beams: the hits follow the plank.
cap.2: Moving L₁ moves every intersection, so the pattern of hits shifts to rays that point higher.
cap.3: Hit set: (s − a)(2s − a − t) ≤ 0 with s ≠ t, i.e. the beam passes between the plank's ends at x = 1 and x = 2. Raising a shifts it.

cap.1: Raise it to the top and the shallow beams all miss; only the steep ones reach. Every peg was answered at once, with no loop over beams.
cap.2: All 64 answers come from one vectorised pass. That is the real lesson of [0.1]: batch the small solves, mask the odd ones.
cap.3: Batched linear algebra with degenerate-case masking: the same pattern as any vectorised op where a few rows are ill-conditioned.

predict.q: A beam runs exactly parallel to a plank. What should your code return for it?

options.t: A miss, caught by checking the determinant first

predict.why: Parallel lines never meet, so the matrix is singular. Detect the near-zero determinant and mark it a miss.

predict.q: The solver says u = 1.2, v = 1.4. Hit or miss?

options.t: Miss: v above 1 is past the plank's far end
Hit: the solver found a crossing

predict.why: The lines do cross, but beyond L₂. The plank only covers v from 0 to 1.

predict.q: The solver says u = -0.8, v = 0.3. Hit or miss?

options.t: Miss: the crossing is behind the torch
Hit: v is inside the plank

predict.why: A ray only goes forwards from its origin, so u must be at least 0.

object.where: Every batched geometry test: collision checks, mesh rendering, and any batch of solves where a few rows are singular.
